# Dew point, not humidity

Ask someone how muggy it is outside and they will tell you the relative humidity. Ask a
meteorologist and they will tell you the dew point. The second number is the useful one, and
the reason is worth understanding.

Relative humidity is a ratio. It tells you how much water vapour the air is holding as a
percentage of the maximum it could hold at its current temperature. That last clause is
where the trouble starts, because the maximum changes with temperature, and it changes a
lot. Warm air holds dramatically more water than cold air.

So relative humidity is a fraction whose denominator moves. Ninety percent at four degrees
in the morning and ninety percent at twenty-eight degrees in the afternoon describe wildly
different amounts of actual moisture. The first is a cool damp dawn. The second is tropical.
A single number that means two different things depending on the temperature is not much use
for comparing one day to another, or one city to another.

The dew point fixes this by measuring the moisture directly, as a temperature. It is the
temperature to which you would have to cool a parcel of air, holding pressure constant, for
it to become saturated and begin condensing. Because it describes the water content itself
rather than a ratio against a moving maximum, it does not shift as the afternoon warms.

That stability is what makes it comparable. A dew point of twenty-one is the same amount of
moisture in the air whether the thermometer reads twenty-four or thirty-four.

The rough scale most people converge on: below ten is dry, and skin and sinuses notice it.
Ten to fifteen is comfortable. Sixteen to eighteen starts to feel sticky. Above twenty is
oppressive, and above twenty-four is the sort of air people remember.

The physiological reason the scale works is sweat. Cooling by evaporation depends on the
gradient between the moisture on your skin and the moisture in the air, and the dew point is
a direct measure of the second quantity. When it climbs above roughly twenty-four, sweat
evaporates slowly enough that the body's main cooling mechanism starts to fail. This is why
heat indices are built from dew point rather than relative humidity, and why a dry
thirty-eight degrees is survivable in a way that a humid thirty-two is not.

There is one more place the distinction earns its keep, which is condensation. Any surface
colder than the dew point will collect water. That is the whole mechanism behind fogged
windows, sweating pipes, and the damp patch in the corner of an exterior wall. If the indoor
dew point is fourteen and a window pane sits at eleven, that window will run with water, and
no amount of wiping addresses the cause. Lower the indoor dew point or raise the surface
temperature.

None of this makes relative humidity useless. It is the right number for anything where the
saturation ratio itself is what matters, which includes most questions about mould growth,
material shrinkage, and static electricity. It is simply the wrong number for the question
people usually ask it, which is whether today will feel worse than yesterday.
